query: Which material can be used for to improve the ductility and toughness of the HfZrTi high-entropy alloy (HEAs), and why?

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small fraction of niobium (Nb) to the HfZrTi high-entropy alloy will improve its ductility and toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A HfZrTi solid‐solution alloy that exhibits limited ductility and toughness under baseline processing conditions.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor addition (e.g., approximately 5 atomic percent) of Nb into the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Process the alloy under conditions comparable to the baseline (e.g., similar melting, casting, and cooling protocols) so that any differences can be attributed to the Nb addition.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a locally modified microstructure, such as a dual-phase structure or enriched grain-boundary regions, where the Nb enhances dislocation mobility.
generation.mechanism: Nb is expected to modify the stacking fault energy and promote dislocation activity. This can contribute to more effective plastic deformation mechanisms (e.g., easier dislocation motion or potential micro-twinning) and improved crack deflection, ultimately enhancing ductility and toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline HfZrTi alloy, the Nb-containing alloy will display higher plastic strain to failure and increased fracture toughness.
generation.baseline: Pure HfZrTi alloy processed under standard conditions with its intrinsic ductility and toughness values.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only within a limited Nb concentration range. Excessive Nb may exceed solubility limits or induce brittle intermetallic phases, negating the improvements.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Nb concentration and the precise quantitative improvement in ductility and toughness are uncertain until experimentally validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of alloys with 0%, 3%, 5%, and 7% Nb added to HfZrTi under identical processing conditions. Subject the samples to tensile tests and fracture toughness measurements while also performing microstructural characterization using SEM/TEM.
measurements: Tensile stress–strain curves (to assess plastic strain to failure and yield strength)
Microstructural analysis (phase distribution and potential formation of brittle intermetallic phases)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-added alloys do not show statistically significant improvements in ductility and toughness compared to the pure HfZrTi alloy, or if brittle phases dominate the microstructure in the Nb-added samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.
